nature-pol-194.title: Extended producer responsibility: makers pay for the waste
nature-pol-194.text: In a 1990 report to the Swedish environment ministry, Thomas Lindhqvist first formally put forward a simple idea: make manufacturers pay for what becomes of their products. Extended producer responsibility, or EPR, holds producers responsible for environmental costs across a product's whole life cycle, mainly the cost of dealing with it as waste. The logic is that brand owners control product design, so they are best placed to cut toxicity and waste. Producers who pay end-of-life costs are pushed to design greener products. EPR can take the form of programs for reuse, buyback or {{ref:nature-eecon-038}}, and producers may pay a producer responsibility organization to handle used products. Unlike {{ref:nature-eecon-034}}, which shares responsibility along the chain, it puts the cost of reprocessing into the product price and relieves local governments. The deposit-refund system is described as based on its principles. In Germany, packaging use per person fell from 94.7 kg to 82 kg between 1991 and 1998 after EPR was adopted, a reduction of 13.4%. A drawback is the administrative burden of rules that differ between countries and waste streams.

nature-pol-229.title: ISO 14000: international standards for environmental management
nature-pol-229.text: As of 2017, there were more than 300,000 ISO 14001 certifications in 171 countries. The ISO 14000 family is a set of international standards for {{ref:nature-gov-100}}, first issued by the International Organization for Standardization in March 1996. The standards help organizations cut their harm to air, water and land, comply with laws and keep improving. Like ISO 9000, they concern how a product or service is made rather than the product itself. ISO 14001 is the core standard. It sets out a framework for such a system but no required level of environmental performance. The series is voluntary, and certification is done by third parties rather than by ISO itself. Firms that adopt it can cut waste, resource use and operating costs, and may gain a competitive advantage. Its predecessor was BS 7750, published in 1992 as the world's first standard of its kind.

nature-pol-226.title: Green industrial policy: governments growing clean industries
nature-pol-226.text: German green industrial policy helped build a renewable energy industry employing over 371,000 people, double the jobs of 2004. Green industrial policy is government strategy to speed the growth of green industries, correcting {{ref:nature-found-045}} and moving toward a {{ref:nature-clim-208}}. The case rests on hard beginnings. Green industries such as renewable energy face high costs and risks, so they need public support until they become commercially viable. New sustainable technologies cannot compete at once with existing ones, because of {{ref:nature-pol-038}}, so governments nurture technological niches. Without government intervention, the market is unlikely to make that shift on its own. Subsidies for a targeted sector are the most common form. Other tools include R&D funding, tax credits, feed-in tariffs, mandates and green buying by governments.

nature-pol-231.title: The Inflation Reduction Act: America's biggest climate law
nature-pol-231.text: The Inflation Reduction Act, a 2022 United States law, is the largest federal legislation ever to address climate change, mainly through tax credits and grants for clean energy. According to the CBO and JCT, it invests $783 billion in {{ref:nature-clim-114}} and climate provisions. Consumers get 10 years of tax credits for heat pumps, rooftop solar and efficient electric heating and cooling. It also created a $27 billion {{ref:nature-clim-091}}, the Greenhouse Gas Reduction Fund, to finance smaller regional ones. After the act, Rhodium Group raised its forecast of 2030 US emission cuts from 17–30% to 29–42% below 2005 levels.

nature-pol-186.title: Ecolabels: the environment on the package
nature-pol-186.text: Germany's Blue Angel, launched in 1978, was the world's first ecolabel. Today the Ecolabel Index counts 456 of them in 199 countries across 25 industry sectors. An ecolabel tells shoppers about a product's environmental impact. Ecolabels are voluntary, whereas green stickers are required by law. Some measure pollution or energy use with scores or units; others certify that a set of minimum practices was followed. Through certification, a farm, forest, fishing operation or mine can show it meets a standard and sell its products as certified. Labels put market pressure on industries to cut their impact, by linking products to the wishes of informed consumers. Trust is the weak spot. Some manufacturers have set up 'rubber stamp' labels to make products look greener than they are ({{ref:nature-nbs-075}}), so shoppers cannot take every label at face value.

nature-pol-236.title: Sustainable seafood guides and labels
nature-pol-236.text: Seafood advisory lists and certification schemes aim to make seafood supply chains transparent and to help shoppers choose seafood from well-managed fish populations. The Marine Stewardship Council, for instance, runs a certification program for consumer seafood products. The economic impact of these schemes is unclear, but they bring non-monetary gains such as better reputation and reorganized supply chains. Their spread has a cost. Many conservationists feel the growing number of seafood labels is confusing consumers.

nature-pol-018.title: Environmental policy: governments taking on environmental problems
nature-pol-018.text: In 1863, after harmful chemical releases caused health problems, the UK adopted the Alkali Act and created the Alkali Inspectorate. It was an early example of environmental policy: a commitment by a government or organization to adopt laws, rules and other measures that deal with environmental problems. Such policy typically covers air and water pollution, waste, ecosystem management, biodiversity, natural resources and endangered species. Its aim is to steer human activity to prevent harm to the environment and to people. Why should government get involved at all? The usual answer is {{ref:nature-found-045}}, such as the free rider problem and the tragedy of the commons. Some problems spur action faster than others. Pollution of air and water tends to move governments more than global warming does, because it causes immediate health problems. Success is judged by how far a policy reduces or solves environmental problems, and whether policies have done so remains debated.

nature-pol-027.title: Market-based instruments: using prices to cut pollution
nature-pol-027.text: David Lloyd George's fuel tax of 1909-1910 may have been Britain's first market-based environmental instrument. Such instruments are policy tools that use markets, prices and other economic signals to give polluters a reason to cut harmful side effects such as pollution. They are also called economic instruments, price-based instruments or new environmental policy instruments. They tackle the market failure of an {{ref:nature-found-031}} in two ways. They charge for external costs through taxes, or they create property rights and a market for using environmental services. Examples include environmental taxes, charges and subsidies, emissions trading, deposit-refund systems, eco-labeling laws and property rights; the EU's emissions trading scheme is one. They differ from voluntary agreements and from command-and-control rules that dictate performance or technology, though they usually still need some regulation. Environmental advocates first opposed them. After successful credit trading in the US lead phasedown, they came to support trading, starting with the acid rain allowance market.

nature-pol-030.title: Public choice: politics without romance
nature-pol-030.text: James Buchanan described public choice as 'politics without romance'. It uses economic tools such as rational choice and {{ref:nature-econ-034}} to study how politicians, officials and voters behave and interact. It stresses that political agents are self-interested, and that collective decisions combine many individual choices. It doubts that government simply maximizes social welfare. Instead it models officials who may also act for their own benefit, as in the budget-maximizing model of bureaucracy. Duncan Black, sometimes called its founding father, laid the groundwork for median voter theory in papers from 1948 to 1958. Its Nobel laureates include Kenneth Arrow, James Buchanan, George Stigler, Gary Becker, Amartya Sen, Vernon Smith and Elinor Ostrom. It has critics. Steven Pressman argues it fails to explain key political behavior, such as why politicians vote against their constituents' interests, or indeed why people vote.

nature-pol-019.title: Rules, prices and persuasion: the three families of policy tools
nature-pol-019.text: Governments carry out environmental policy with three main families of tools: regulation, economic instruments and persuasion. Regulation sets rules, often backed by law, that ban, require or limit behavior. Pollution limits and bans on hazardous substances are examples. Critics call it a top-down 'command and control' approach, because it leaves little choice in how goals are met. Economic instruments work through incentives instead: taxes, fees, subsidies, and markets for trading rights in pollutants or resources such as SO2, CO2, water and fishing quotas. They assume people act mainly from rational self-interest, a premise that studies of decision-making cast doubt on. The third family, normative or 'hortatory' instruments, relies on persuasion and information. Awareness campaigns and voluntary agreements with businesses belong here.

nature-pol-020.title: Which tool works best? The instrument debate
nature-pol-020.text: Market instruments are often promoted as a more efficient, cost-effective alternative to regulation. Not everyone is convinced. Many analysts argue that regulation, incentives, market instruments, taxes and subsidies can achieve the same results. Kemp and Pontoglio found no evidence that market-based approaches are better for eco-innovation, and some evidence that regulation spurs more radical innovation. Hahn called the performance of economic instruments 'not very impressive', and Tietenberg concluded they are 'no panacea'. Efficiency is not the only test. Instruments differ in how costs and benefits are shared, so distributional, ethical and political aspects matter too. That helps explain some choices. Tradeable permits handed to resource users are generally preferred by affected industries, which helps explain their popularity since the rise of neoliberalism. Analysts still disagree whether market instruments are truly more efficient and innovation-friendly, or simply spread costs differently.

nature-pol-028.title: Taxes or tradable permits: price certainty versus quantity certainty
nature-pol-028.text: A pollution tax fixes the cost of cutting pollution; a tradable permit system fixes the total amount allowed. Each choice has consequences. A permit system sets a cap and is likely to reach it more cheaply than other means, possibly undershooting it as technology improves. A tax has no cap. The pollution cut depends on the rate chosen, which can be adjusted until the incentive works best. Taxes have lower compliance costs than permits but are less reliable at hitting a target quantity. Tax revenue can be used to cut other distorting taxes, a possible 'double dividend', though less pollution also means less revenue. Permits can be auctioned or handed out free by grandfathering. Critics say formal emission rights amount to a license to pollute.

nature-pol-026.title: Induced innovation: expensive inputs spur new inventions
nature-pol-026.text: In 1932, in The Theory of Wages, John Hicks proposed that when one input becomes relatively more expensive, firms are spurred to invent ways of using less of it. The classic illustration is higher wages encouraging labor-saving inventions. The idea has been applied to rising energy costs speeding up energy efficiency. Global GDP and CO2 emissions grew together until the 1970s, when sharp oil price rises cut consumption. After the oil shock, investment in alternative energy, efficient cars and heating meant CO2 grew more slowly than GDP, even after petrol prices fell in the 1980s. Farming shows the same pattern: when scarce inputs such as land rise in price, farmers seek technologies that use more abundant inputs instead. Not every model captures it. The DICE climate model treats innovation as external, so it leaves out induced technological change.

nature-pol-022.title: Environmental policy analysis: three ways to study policy
nature-pol-022.text: Environmental policy analysis is the academic study of how environmental policies are made, how well they work and how they could be improved. It has three main approaches. The analycentric or rational approach uses mainly quantitative methods to find the most cost-effective solution, favoring tools such as cost-benefit analysis, taxes and tradable permits. The policy process approach stresses politics and power, tracing steps from agenda setting through implementation to evaluation. The meta-policy approach studies how institutions, culture, economic systems and discourses shape policymaking.

nature-pol-023.title: Environmental policy integration: the environment in every policy
nature-pol-023.text: Transport, farming and trade policies all affect the environment. Environmental policy integration holds that policies in every area should take account of their effects on the environment and on other areas. The idea has been discussed since the 1980s, under names such as policy mainstreaming, policy coordination and holistic governance.

nature-pol-025.title: Implicit carbon prices: charging for carbon without saying so
nature-pol-025.text: Almost every country taxes gasoline, but only 39 have explicit carbon pricing. A fuel tax is an implicit carbon price: a cost on greenhouse gas emissions imposed indirectly, by a measure that changes the cost of emitting without targeting carbon itself. Explicit carbon prices, such as carbon taxes and emissions trading, target emissions directly. Implicit and explicit prices together make the effective carbon price. Implicit prices can also be negative. Fuel taxes raise the cost of emitting, but fossil fuel subsidies make emitting cheaper. Implicit prices spread more easily, because they tackle local problems, need less administrative capacity and face less political opposition. The difference matters at borders. The EU's border carbon adjustment counts only explicit prices, while a proposed US version would include implicit ones.

nature-pol-033.title: Constitutional economics: agreeing on the rules of the game
nature-pol-033.text: Constitutional economics applies public choice and political economy to the design of constitutional rules. Buchanan and Tullock argued that for government to benefit everyone, people must agree on the rules, not on every government action. They split decisions into two kinds. Constitutional decisions set lasting rules. Political decisions are made within those rules.

nature-pol-032.title: Rational ignorance: why many voters stay uninformed
nature-pol-032.text: Even in a close election, the chance that one vote decides the result is effectively zero. So the expected gain from voting is near zero too. Rational ignorance is the theory that a self-interested voter may therefore sensibly choose not to vote or get informed. Anthony Downs argued in An Economic Theory of Democracy that for many citizens, rational behavior means investing nothing in political information.

nature-pol-029.title: Markets or mandates: flexible tools versus fixed rules
nature-pol-029.text: Command-and-control rules often set the same emission limit for every firm, even though some can cut pollution cheaply and others only at high cost. Market instruments do not dictate technology or equal cuts for every firm, which gives firms more flexibility. Critics also say command and control blocks innovation, though empirical studies show external price changes can induce it. Others see roles where rules work better than markets: where regulators lack information, where trading markets are too thin, or where emissions have purely local impacts.

nature-pol-021.title: Policy mix: combining tools that do not clash
nature-pol-021.text: Environmental problems have many aspects, so several policy instruments may be needed together. Such a combination is a policy mix. The measures should be designed not to undermine each other, since overlapping policies add unnecessary administrative costs. In macroeconomics the term has a narrower meaning: the combination of a country's monetary policy, set by the central bank, and its fiscal policy, set by the government.

nature-pol-024.title: Gossen's second law: getting the most from a budget
nature-pol-024.text: Gossen's second law, named after Hermann Heinrich Gossen (1810–1858), says a person gets the most from a budget by spending so that the extra satisfaction per unit of money is equal across all goods. Suppose the last unit of money spent on one good bought less extra satisfaction than it could have bought elsewhere. Then the person would do better to switch. Formally, the law follows from maximizing utility under a {{ref:nature-econ-102}} with Lagrange multipliers.

nature-pol-034.title: Lobbying: influencing the people who make the rules
nature-pol-034.text: Firms that spent most on lobbying relative to their assets earned 'blistering' returns, a 2011 study found. Lobbying is legal advocacy that tries to influence decisions made by legislators, regulators or sometimes judges. Its main form is meeting lawmakers directly, armed with research, data and draft proposals. Lobbyists can be individuals, corporations, nonprofits, interest groups and political action committees. Inside lobbying deals with decision-makers directly; outside lobbying pressures them by mobilizing public opinion. Research documents three effects: trading money for access, persuading officials with information, and mobilizing citizens or coalitions. Lobbying can pull politicians away from the median voter, especially when special-interest money is high and public attention low. It can also encourage lax enforcement of laws. Many governments require lobbyists to register and disclose spending, clients and issues. Its ethics remain disputed: defenders call it legitimate advocacy, critics say it corrupts the law for private interests.

nature-pol-042.title: Rent-seeking: getting richer without creating wealth
nature-pol-042.text: Robert Shiller's classic example is a landowner who chains a river and charges passing boats to lower the chain. The landowner adds no value. That is rent-seeking: increasing one's wealth by manipulating public policy or economic conditions, without creating new wealth. 'Rent' here means economic rent, income beyond what is needed to keep a factor in its current use. Profit-seeking creates wealth through mutually beneficial trade; rent-seeking only redistributes existing wealth. Typical examples are lobbying for subsidies, tariffs, quotas or rules that hobble competitors. The costs are broad. Rent-seeking wastes resources, stifles competition, lowers wealth creation and government revenue, and raises inequality and corruption risk. Money spent on lobbyists rather than research or equipment slows growth, and Mancur Olson argued that countries dominated by organized interest groups lose vitality and decline. Critics note it can be hard to tell beneficial profit-seeking from harmful rent-seeking.

nature-pol-038.title: Path dependence: why history matters
nature-pol-038.text: More than half the world's railways use the 143.5 cm standard gauge, inherited from early coal tramways. That is path dependence: past events or decisions constrain later ones, so that 'history matters' for where a system ends up. Economists developed the idea to explain how technologies are adopted and industries evolve. A path-dependent process may settle into one of several equilibria, depending on its starting point and chance events. Simple neoclassical models allow only one outcome. Drivers include lock-in, positive feedback, increasing returns and self-reinforcement. Paul David argued in 1985 that a first-to-market standard such as the QWERTY keyboard can become entrenched even if inferior. Liebowitz and Margolis reply that inefficient lock-in is rare, with no real-world private cases, and economists still argue the point. The idea reaches nature too: commercial fisheries' harvest rates are path dependent, because institutions adapt slowly while ecosystems change fast.

nature-pol-040.title: Regulatory capture: when the watchdog serves the watched
nature-pol-040.text: After the 2010 Deepwater Horizon oil spill, the US Minerals Management Service was widely cited as a captured regulator. Regulatory capture is when a regulator or policymaker is co-opted to serve a small group, such as an industry, instead of the public. A special interest is put ahead of the general public, causing a net loss for society. The cause is lopsided stakes. Groups with high stakes focus resources on regulation, while the dispersed public, each with little at stake, does not. George Stigler, a Nobel laureate economist, was a major developer of the theory. A captured regulator can be worse than no regulation, because it wields government authority; transparency may reduce the damage. Smaller government units are easier for concentrated industries to capture, as when timber states block national policy. Water management in Australia's Murray–Darling Basin has been analyzed as a case of rent-seeking and capture.

nature-pol-036.title: The median voter theorem: why the middle wins
nature-pol-036.text: Line up voters and candidates along one left-right spectrum, and majority-rule voting elects the candidate the middle, or median, voter prefers. That is the median voter theorem. Voters are assumed to rank candidates by closeness, so the candidate nearest the median voter beats every rival by a majority. Duncan Black first derived it in 1948, and Kenneth Arrow independently. With two candidates a simple majority vote satisfies it; with more, any Condorcet method does. In more than one dimension there may be no majority winner, as the McKelvey–Schofield chaos theorem shows. The theorem is popular in political economy because it yields testable links between voters and policy. The tests are not kind. Levitt (1996) found senators from the same state but different parties voted only slightly more alike than random pairs, and studies from India also contradict its predictions.

nature-pol-035.title: The fossil fuels lobby: big money against climate rules
nature-pol-035.text: Fossil fuel interests spent $2 billion on climate-change lobbying in the US from 2000 to 2016, many times what citizens and environmentalists spent. The fossil fuels lobby is the paid representatives of oil, gas and coal companies and related industries such as chemicals, plastics and aviation. Their wealth and economic importance give them the means to seek outsized influence. The lobby promotes climate change denial, obstructs environmental and climate policy and works to keep fossil fuel subsidies. Its reach is global. The five biggest oil and gas companies spent at least 251 million euros lobbying the EU on climate policy since 2010. According to the UNFCCC, 636 fossil fuel lobbyists attended COP27. In Canada, fossil fuel lobbyists contacted officials five times more than environmental groups between 2011 and 2018. The lobby has used crises such as COVID-19 and the 2022 invasion of Ukraine to try to roll back regulations.

nature-pol-044.title: The logic of collective action: why small groups win
nature-pol-044.text: In 1965 Mancur Olson's book The Logic of Collective Action argued that small groups with concentrated interests win out over large groups with diffuse interests. The reason is the {{ref:nature-econ-617}}. Members of any group providing a public good are tempted to free ride on others' efforts. Large groups face higher organizing costs, and each member gains less, so they are less able to act. Without selective incentives, collective action is unlikely even among large groups with shared interests. A minority bound by concentrated incentives can therefore dominate the majority. Critics dispute parts of the argument. Susanne Lohmann notes the US sugar import quota created 2,261 jobs while reducing overall welfare, and blames information asymmetry rather than free riding. Gunnar Trumbull counters that diffuse interests such as consumers can win through a 'legitimacy premium' and coalitions.

nature-pol-043.title: The Tullock paradox: why political favors come so cheap
nature-pol-043.text: A rent-seeker hoping to gain a billion dollars may need to spend merely ten million, about 1% of the gain. The Tullock paradox is this puzzle: political favors can be bought for far less than they are worth to the buyer. Proposed explanations include voters punishing lavish politicians, competition among politicians to offer favors, and lack of trust in illicit deals.

nature-pol-039.title: Critical junctures: moments that set a lasting course
nature-pol-039.text: A critical juncture is a moment when contingent choices set an institution on a path of development that is hard to reverse. Ruth and David Collier made the framework prominent in political science. It has been used to explain the rise and persistence of welfare states, and differences in economic development between countries. Kathleen Thelen warns that such frameworks are too deterministic, since institutions keep evolving.

nature-pol-041.title: Money or mindset: two types of regulatory capture
nature-pol-041.text: Regulatory capture comes in two basic types. Materialist, or financial, capture is driven by the regulator's self-interest. It can result from bribery, revolving doors between regulator and industry, political donations or a regulator's wish to keep its funding. The top 5 financial companies account for around 80% of revolving-door movements, so big firms do most capturing. Non-materialist, or cognitive, capture is driven by biased views. Specialized technical industries risk this cultural capture, because regulators must hire experts who mostly come from the industry.

nature-pol-045.title: Bootleggers and Baptists: strange allies behind a rule
nature-pol-045.text: Sunday alcohol bans won support from Baptist activists, and from bootleggers, who sold more when legal sales were restricted. Bruce Yandle turned this into a general idea: regulations win support both from groups that want their stated purpose and from groups that profit from undermining it. The 'Baptists' take the moral high ground and give politicians cover, while the 'bootleggers' lobby quietly behind closed doors. The theory predicts that coalitions of opposing interests agreeing on one rule succeed more often than one-sided groups. Such coalitions tend to produce suboptimal laws; a surtax on Sunday sales, for instance, could cut drinking as much as a ban. Yandle and Buck applied it to the {{ref:nature-clim-056}}: environmental groups gave moral support while corporations and nations sought advantage over rivals. Smith and Yandle later distinguished covert, noncooperative, cooperative and coordinated patterns. The idea has not been systematically tested, and remains a useful catch-phrase rather than an accepted principle.

nature-pol-037.title: The Hotelling–Downs model: parties drifting to the middle
nature-pol-037.text: In 1929 Hotelling described a principle of minimum differentiation in business competition. Anthony Downs applied it to politics in 1957. The Hotelling–Downs model predicts that politicians who care only about winning will move to the median voter's position. In a two-party system, both parties drift toward the median voter. Reality often breaks the conditions. Primaries and most voting rules in national use do so, so candidates may not converge.

openers.choosing-among-instruments: Environmental policy is a government's commitment to deal with environmental problems, but commitment is only the start: it must pick its tools. They come in families: regulation, economic instruments that use prices and markets, and persuasion. Analysts still debate which works best, and whether a pollution tax, fixing the cost of cuts, beats a permit system, fixing the total. Rising costs can even spur firms to invent ways of using less of a costly input. Public choice adds a warning, studying politicians, officials and voters as self-interested actors, some of whom sensibly stay uninformed.
openers.political-economy-of-environmental-polic: Environmental rules are made by people, and people have interests. Lobbying tries to influence lawmakers and regulators, and the fossil fuels lobby is among the best funded. Small groups with concentrated interests often beat large groups with diffuse ones, and a regulator can be captured by the industry it oversees. Elections pull candidates toward the median voter, while past decisions constrain later ones, so history matters. This chapter explains why good policy on paper can be hard to pass, and harder still to keep.

reviews.choosing-among-instruments: Environmental policy can rely on rules, prices or persuasion, and this chapter showed that none wins every time. Market instruments promise flexibility and lower costs, yet studies find regulation can match them and sometimes spur more radical innovation. Taxes give certainty about cost, permits certainty about quantity, and implicit prices such as fuel taxes add a hidden layer to both. Because problems have many aspects, governments combine tools in a policy mix. Public choice reminds the reader that the people choosing these tools have interests of their own.
reviews.political-economy-of-environmental-polic: The theories in this chapter explain why environmental policy is shaped by more than evidence. Rent-seeking and lobbying let concentrated interests buy favors cheaply, as the Tullock paradox notes, while the logic of collective action leaves the diffuse public poorly organized. Captured regulators, whether by money or by mindset, can serve the industries they watch. Path dependence and critical junctures explain why choices, once made, are hard to reverse. Yet unlikely coalitions of bootleggers and Baptists show that rules can still pass when moral and money interests align.
